lead: A stretched strut, a bent spar and a twisted control rod all store energy, like a wound spring. For a linearly elastic member the stored energy is one half the load times the deflection that load causes. Written in closed form for axial, bending and torsion loading, that single number gives deflections of trusses and beams without tracing the full elastic curve. Designers use it to compare competing layouts — a strut, a spar, a torque tube — long before any detail drawing exists.
prereq: You need: stress, strain, Young’s modulus, shear modulus, second moment of area, and the bending moment diagram of a beam.

sections.h3: Work done by the load is stored in the member

blocks.text: Load a member and it deflects. In a linearly elastic member the deflection grows in exact proportion to the load, and on removal the member springs back. The load has done work, and that work sits inside the material as strain energy U, measured in joules (1 J = 1 N·m).
Plot load against deflection. The graph is a straight line from the origin to the point (Δ, P). The work done is the area under that line.

blocks.where: P is the final load in newtons, Δ the deflection at that load in metres, U the stored strain energy in joules.

blocks.text: The ½ is there because the load does not start at P. It climbs from zero to P, so the average load along the way is P/2. A load of the same final size applied suddenly (constant force, no initial velocity) gives twice the deflection and stress, so it stores four times this energy. A true impact or dropped weight is a separate case. Exam questions assume gradual loading.
Strain energy is a scalar: no direction, never negative. It is quadratic in the loads, so energies of separate load cases do not simply add.
Typical questions: how much energy does this landing gear leg absorb? Does this spar store more energy than that one? Energy methods answer both without solving the deflection everywhere.

sections.h3: Three closed forms: axial, bending, torsion

blocks.text: Each mode is ½ × load × deformation, rewritten using section properties.

blocks.where: P is the constant axial force (N), L the member length (m), A the cross-section area (m²), E Young's modulus (Pa); U comes out in joules.
M is the bending moment at station x (N·m), I the second moment of area about the neutral axis of bending (m⁴), x runs along the beam (m).
T is the torque (N·m), G the shear modulus (Pa), J the polar second moment of area (m⁴). For a solid circular shaft of diameter d, J = πd⁴/32.

blocks.text: For a stepped bar or a shaft with several torques, split it into segments, take each segment as constant, and add: U = Σ Pᵢ²Lᵢ/(2AᵢEᵢ), and likewise for torsion. For a varying moment, integrate.

sections.h3: Standard beam results, resilience, and what is left out

blocks.text: Two beam answers are quoted so often that they are worth deriving once.

items: Cantilever, tip load P, length L: measure x from the free end, so M(x) = Px.
Integrate from 0 to L: P²/(2EI) × L³/3 = P²L³/(6EI).
Simply supported beam, central load P: with x measured from the left support, M = Px/2 (valid for 0 ≤ x ≤ L/2).
Integrate 0 to L/2, then double: 2 × P²/(8EI) × (L/2)³/3 = P²L³/(96EI).

blocks.text: Both grow as P², so doubling the load quadruples the stored energy. Bending energy grows as L³ while axial energy grows only as L — a long beam is a spring, a long strut is not.

Modulus of resilience is strain energy per unit volume (J/m³); resilience itself is a total energy in joules. Proof resilience is the total energy stored at the yield load, the most the member can hold without permanent set. For axial loading the modulus of resilience is σy²/(2E).

Shear strain energy from the shear force V is deliberately left out here; it matters in short deep beams and thin webs. Torsion of non-circular and thin-walled sections needs shear flow and is treated with thin-walled sections.

examples.question: (a) An aluminium alloy strut of length L = 1.2 m, cross-section area A = 250 mm² and E = 70 GPa carries a constant axial load P = 20 kN. Find its extension and the strain energy stored. (b) A steel cantilever 2 m long, E = 200 GPa, I = 8 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, carries a tip load of 1 kN. Find its strain energy. Assume linear elasticity and gradually applied loads.
steps: Convert to base units: A = 250 mm² = 250 × 10⁻⁶ m², E = 70 GPa = 70 × 10⁹ Pa, P = 20 kN = 20 000 N.
Energy from the area under the load-deflection line: U = ½PΔ = ½ × 20 000 × 1.371 × 10⁻³ = 13.71 J.
Same answer from the formula: U = P²L/(2AE) = (20 000)² × 1.2/(2 × 250 × 10⁻⁶ × 70 × 10⁹) = 4.8 × 10⁸/(3.5 × 10⁷) = 13.71 J. Units: N²·m/(m²·N/m²) = N·m = J.
Check the cantilever with the triangle rule: its tip deflection is Δ = PL³/(3EI) = 1000 × 8/(3 × 1.6 × 10⁶) = 1.667 × 10⁻³ m, so U = ½PΔ = ½ × 1000 × 1.667 × 10⁻³ = 0.833 J, the same as the formula.
examples.answer: The strut stores U = 13.71 J with an extension of 1.371 mm, and the cantilever stores U = 0.83 J.

traps: Writing U = PΔ and dropping the ½. The load grew from zero, so the average is P/2; forgetting it doubles every answer.
Putting I into the torsion formula. J is polar: J = πd⁴/32 for a solid circle. It equals 2I only for a circular section, never in general.
Adding the strain energies of two separate load cases. Energy is quadratic in load, so two loads acting together give extra cross terms.
Feeding mm² or GPa straight into the formula. Convert A to m² (×10⁻⁶) and E to Pa (×10⁹), or you are out by 10³ or more.
Applying P²L/(2AE) to a stepped or tapered bar without splitting it into constant segments or integrating.

quiz.q: Define strain energy and give its SI unit.
quiz.a: Strain energy U is the work done by a gradually applied load in deforming an elastic member, stored within it and recoverable on unloading. Unit: joule, 1 J = 1 N·m.

quiz.q: Why does U = ½PΔ carry the factor ½?
quiz.a: The load rises from zero to P while the deflection rises from zero to Δ, both in proportion. Work is the area of the load-deflection triangle, ½ × base × height = ½PΔ.

quiz.q: State the strain energy of a circular shaft in torsion and explain why the polar second moment appears.
quiz.a: U = T²L/(2GJ). Torque twists the section about its axis, so each element's resistance depends on its distance from that axis; J = ∫r²dA measures exactly that, whereas I is taken about a diameter.

quiz.q: A bar of length 2 m, area 400 mm², E = 200 GPa carries 50 kN axially. Find U.
A simply supported beam of span 4 m, I = 40 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, E = 200 GPa, carries a central load of 20 kN. Find U.
Two beams have the same span, material, load and rectangular cross-section width; the second has twice the depth of the first. Compare their stored energies.
quiz.a: For a rectangular section I = bd³/12, so with the same breadth b, I scales as depth cubed; the deeper beam has 8I. Since U = P²L³/(96EI), the energy of the deeper beam is one eighth of the shallower one: it is stiffer and stores less for the same load.

quiz.q: For the aluminium strut of the worked example, what axial load doubles the stored energy?
quiz.a: U ∝ P², so doubling U needs P√2 = 20 × 1.414 = 28.28 kN. The extension also rises by √2, to 1.94 mm, and the stress must still stay below yield.

quiz.q: A solid steel control rod of diameter 12 mm and length 1.5 m carries a torque of 40 N·m. G = 80 GPa. Find the strain energy stored.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every finite element stiffness matrix is built from these same integrals: the element energy ½uᵀku is the bending integral written in matrix form. The energy release rate of fracture mechanics, G = −dU/dA, comes from differentiating stored energy with respect to crack area. Landing gear oleo sizing and crash-energy absorbers are strain-energy budgets in industry. Search next for complementary energy, the J-integral, and strain energy density.
